title: Actuation Lite: proposal + SDK playbook (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This doc is an iterative product proposal for a lightweight actuation protocol ("Actuation Lite") and an SDK playbook that together aim to simplify the most common hosted API patterns: incremental streaming, explicit tool invocation (tool-calling), and reliably shaped structured output for downstream consumers. Intention: provide a low-friction surface for app developers who need predictable client behaviour and simple SDK ergonomics while preserving the advanced server-side features (fallbacks, batching, caching).

Why this exists (problem statement):
- Teams building chat + tool workflows repeatedly struggle with three friction points: (1) poor client ergonomics around partial/streamed responses and tool handoffs; (2) brittle structured output contracts when generation deviates; (3) complexities of SDKs trying to support both maximum flexibility and simple defaults.
- Current hosted API proposals are powerful but have a high cognitive cost for engineers shipping 80% of use cases (search+compose, simple tool invocations, form-fills, code edits). We want a pragmatic "lite" surface that avoids full-on frame protocols and complex back-and-forth state.

Goals (measurable):
- Ship an API surface + SDK defaults that let a developer implement a streaming chat with tool calls in under 2 hours using examples and a single SDK import.
- Reduce integration debugging tickets by 30% for tool-call patterns (measured via internal CS triage tags) in the first quarter after rollout.
- Provide a structured-output "safety fallback" so downstream parsers/validators can detect invalid payloads and request a deterministic regeneration flow.

Non-goals:
- Not trying to replace the full typed-frame / session-mosaic designs. Actuation Lite is intentionally opinionated and constrained.
- Not supporting advanced multi-party tool-federations or microtransaction semantics out of the box.

High-level approach (proposal):
1) Define a compact actuation envelope for streaming bytes that fits into existing response streaming pipeline (minimize runtime churn).
  - Envelope types: partial_text, tool_request, tool_response_attachment, structured_commit, ephemeral_meta
  - Each envelope is a small JSON line that precedes content chunks when necessary. Plain-text chunks are sent unchanged when no envelope is active.
2) Introduce a single SDK primitive: Actuator (client-side helper). The Actuator exposes 3 core calls: startStream(), onToolInvoke(handler), finalizeStructured(commitSchema).
  - startStream(): returns a composable async iterator that yields either text chunks or envelope objects.
  - onToolInvoke(handler): registers a callback that receives tool_request envelopes and is responsible for fulfilling them synchronously or via the network; the SDK will surface helper utilities to auto-serialize to/from common connector shapes (http, sql, lambda).
  - finalizeStructured(commitSchema): attempts to validate the final structured output against a simple schema; if validation fails, an automated deterministic "repair request" is emitted to the server for re-generation using the same context and a tight retry budget.
3) Server-side behavior:
  - Lightweight tool handshake: server emits tool_request with: id, tool_name, args_preview (short), optional sync_hint (can this be served synchronously without user action?).
  - If client can fulfill, it returns tool_response_attachment with correlation id. Server may continue streaming while waiting up to a configurable timeout, otherwise will yield a structured fallback path (see safety fallback).
  - Structured commits: server marks the message boundary with structured_commit that includes schema_id and serialized payload. The Actuator triggers validation.

API surface (examples):
- HTTP streaming + envelopes (pseudo):
  GET /v1/streams?model=redwood-lite&session=xyz
  -> chunk: "Hello, here is a summary..."
  -> chunk: <JSON-LINE {"type":"tool_request","id":"t-77","tool":"calendar.create","args_preview":"{\"date\":\"2026-03-01\"...}"}>
  -> chunk: "Continuing narrative while awaiting tool..." (server can interleave)
  -> chunk: <JSON-LINE {"type":"tool_response_attachment","id":"t-77","status":"ok","response_summary":"created event id e-9"}>
  -> chunk: <JSON-LINE {"type":"structured_commit","schema":"form-v1","payload": "{...}"}>

SDK ergonomics (principles):
- Minimal surface area: one Actuator class with small set of helpers. Avoid exposing low-level streaming frames by default (advanced devs can opt in). - Good defaults: auto-retry for fast connector failures, compact debug logs, human-readable telemetry (token cost per envelope).
- Progressive disclosure: advanced APIs for typed frames, manual checkpointing, and snapshot replay but they are in separate modules so beginner UX stays tiny.
- Cross-language parity: keep primitives mappable to JS/Go/Python idioms (AsyncIterator in JS, iterator/generator in Python, channel-like stream in Go).

Structured output contract and safety fallback:
- Commit schema registry: small registry of canonical schema ids (form-v1, action-v1, sql-rowset-v1). Each schema is intentionally simple (top-level typed fields, optional free_text note). - Validation step: Actuator.validate(commit) uses JSON Schema-lite rules (type checks, required fields, enums). If validation fails, Actuator emits a deterministic repair request to server in a "repair" envelope that includes failing_fields and failure_context.
- Repair request semantics: server will perform at most one repair pass under the same generation context (to avoid infinite loops). If still invalid, server emits structured_commit with status:invalid and an explanation string; SDK surfaces this as a client-side error to the integrator.

Backward compatibility and migration story: guide for customers:
- Default routing: legacy clients receive plain text streaming with minimal change. Actuation Lite is opt-in via a request header X-Actuation: lite or SDK negotiation.
- Incremental rollout: begin with beta for customers using simple tool-call patterns (CS-tracked cohort). Provide a migration CLI that converts existing webhooks/handlers to the Actuator shim.

Telemetry and observability:
- Emit per-envelope metrics: envelope_count_by_type, avg-latency-tool-response, structured_validation_failures, repair_invocations.
- Add sample traces in Console: show timeline of stream with markers for tool_request / tool_response / structured_commit and cost deltas.

Operational constraints and SLO considerations:
- Actuation timeouts: default synchronous tool timeout 3s, max 10s configurable per customer. If tool not returned within timeout server will either yield a best-effort placeholder or switch to fallback model variant (lower latency but less context).
- Batching and KV cache compatibility: tool_request/state should be serializable into KV cache; avoid large binary attachments in the Actuation Lite lane.

Developer experience: examples + quickstart (notes to self):
- JS quickstart skeleton:
  const a = new Actuator({apiKey: process.env.RW_KEY});
  const stream = await a.startStream({model: 'redwood-lite', prompt: 'Plan a 30min meeting'});
  for await (const chunk of stream) {
    if (chunk.type === 'text') renderText(chunk.data);
    if (chunk.type === 'tool_request') {
      const resp = await myCalendar.create(chunk.args);
      await a.sendToolResponse(chunk.id, resp);
    }
    if (chunk.type === 'structured_commit') {
      const ok = await a.finalizeStructured(chunk.schema, chunk.payload);
      if (!ok) showRepairUI();
    }
  }
- Provide sample server-side adapter for common SaaS connectors (Calendar, Email, DB).

Open questions / trade-offs (recording for scoping meeting):
- Should we permit multiple repair passes automatically? risk: loops and higher cost. Initial stance: single auto-repair only.
- How much of the envelope validation/repair should be visible to customers vs. abstracted? (visibility helps debugging but increases surface area).
- How to prioritize envelopes in low-bandwidth mobile contexts: drop ephemeral_meta vs. block on tool_response? (offer client-side priority hints).
- Failure modes: if tool_response arrives after structured_commit, should server accept late correlation and annotate, or treat as orphan? prefer annotate with footnote for now.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (now -> 6 weeks): internal prototype + JS SDK experiment with two internal apps (support-bot, doc-editor).
- Phase 1 (6–12 weeks): beta with 3 external customers; add Console visualization hooks.
- Phase 2 (12–20 weeks): public SDK release (JS + Python), production monitor dashboards and default timeouts set by plan.

Next steps (owners + quick tasks):
- Maya: produce a small JS prototype and add to examples repo (due 2025-12-05).
- Diego: spec server-envelope wire format and update streaming runtime compatibility matrix (due 2025-12-12).
- Priya: draft Console visual trace wireframe + telemetry panel (due 2025-12-19).
- Avery: draft SDK API docs and migration guide (due 2025-12-19).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally opinionated and aims to cover the "80%" case. Looking for feedback on (a) timeouts; (b) schema-lite surface; (c) how much to surface repair flows in SDK (UI hooks vs low-level events).

Slack snippets and references (quick):
- thread: https://slack.redwood.com/hosted-api/actuation-lite-2025
- initial experiment: github.com/redwood-inference/examples/actuation-lite-demo

Unresolved:
- canonical schema storage location (Confluence vs new Schema Registry)
- exact encoding for args_preview (stringified vs partial typed).

End of draft.
